Family Health

Treating hormone-related symptoms: what the options actually do

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Treatment works best when it addresses a diagnosed cause and a clear symptom. Hormone replacement, contraception, metabolic medicines and everyday comfort measures have different roles; none is a universal solution for everything described as a hormonal imbalance.

Start with the cause, not a promise to balance everything

Hormones carry signals between organs. Their levels normally change with puberty, menstrual cycles, pregnancy and ageing. A persistent excess or deficiency can also reflect a medical condition, but tiredness, weight change, acne or low sexual desire alone cannot identify which hormone is involved. These symptoms have many possible causes.

Treatment may replace a missing hormone, reduce a hormone’s production or effects, address a separate underlying illness, or relieve a particular symptom. There is no single treatment for every problem described as a hormonal imbalance. A useful consultation begins with the symptoms, their timing, medicines and supplements, relevant examination and targeted tests.

Systemic oestrogen for menopausal symptoms

Menopausal hormone therapy can help troublesome hot flushes and night sweats. Oestrogen may be given through a tablet, patch, gel or another suitable formulation. The choice depends on the symptoms, medical history, preferences and local products rather than simply choosing the strongest dose.

People who still have a uterus usually need a progestogen alongside systemic oestrogen to protect the uterine lining. Risks vary with personal history, preparation and route. Treatment requires a benefit-and-risk discussion and follow-up; it is not a general rejuvenation treatment or a remedy for every symptom occurring around menopause.

Local treatment for vaginal dryness

Vaginal oestrogen comes in preparations such as creams, tablets and rings. It can help vaginal dryness and discomfort when low oestrogen is contributing. Low-dose local treatment has much less systemic absorption than treatment intended to act throughout the body, but it is still a medicine with prescribing considerations.

It does not generally treat hot flushes. Low-dose vaginal oestrogen usually does not require the same additional progestogen as systemic treatment, but discuss your own history, especially unexplained bleeding or hormone-sensitive cancer. Lubricants and vaginal moisturisers are separate non-hormonal options and may also be helpful.

Hormonal contraception and cycle symptoms

Hormonal contraception includes combined or progestin-only pills, patches, injections, vaginal rings and hormonal intrauterine devices. These methods can change bleeding patterns and may be used to manage some menstrual symptoms as well as prevent pregnancy. They do not all contain the same hormones or have the same effects.

Selected combined pills may help acne and excess androgen-related hair growth. A hormonal intrauterine device may help control bleeding, but should not be assumed to treat acne or facial hair in the same way. Choosing a method requires attention to clot risk, migraine history, blood pressure, other medicines and pregnancy plans.

Anti-androgens for selected skin and hair concerns

Androgens are present in all sexes. When their effects contribute to excess facial or body hair, acne or some forms of scalp hair thinning, a clinician may consider treatment that reduces those effects. A blood test is only part of the assessment: symptoms can occur without a markedly raised circulating androgen level.

Anti-androgen medicines have different indications and monitoring needs. Some can harm fetal development, so reliable pregnancy prevention and a plan for stopping before conception may be necessary. Do not start a product sold as a hormone blocker without checking what it contains and whether it is suitable for you.

Testosterone is for a defined clinical indication

Testosterone treatment may help some men with symptoms and repeatedly confirmed low testosterone caused by an appropriate medical condition. Diagnosis needs correctly timed measurements and investigation of the cause, rather than a single low result or tiredness alone. Treatment may use a gel, injection or another locally available preparation.

It can suppress sperm production and is generally inappropriate when trying to conceive in the near term. It also needs monitoring and is unsuitable in certain medical circumstances. Delayed puberty in an adolescent is a different specialist assessment; it should not be managed using an adult supplement or a relative’s prescription.

Thyroid hormone replacement

An underactive thyroid is commonly treated with levothyroxine, a replacement for thyroid hormone. Brand names such as Synthroid, Levoxyl or Unithroid are market-specific examples, not different cures for a general hormonal imbalance. The dose is adjusted using blood tests and clinical circumstances.

Tell the prescriber about supplements, other medicines and how you take the tablet, because absorption and interactions can affect results. Do not change the dose to try to lose weight. If you become pregnant, contact the treating team promptly: thyroid monitoring and dose needs may change, and treatment should not simply be stopped.

Metformin has a specific metabolic role

Metformin is widely used in type 2 diabetes and may also be prescribed for selected people with polycystic ovary syndrome, traditionally called PCOS. An international name change announced in 2026 uses polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, or PMOS; both names may still appear in records and local services.

In this syndrome, metformin may be considered for metabolic concerns and, in some circumstances, cycle or ovulation management. It is not automatically the best medicine for every symptom, and it is not a universal hormone reset. Gastrointestinal effects, kidney function, longer-term monitoring and the reason for treatment belong in the prescribing discussion.

Medicines for distressing low sexual desire

Low desire can relate to pain, stress, sleep, medicines, relationships, mental health or a medical condition. A drug is not automatically the answer. Flibanserin, sold as Addyi in the US, and injectable bremelanotide, sold as Vyleesi, have specific indications for acquired, generalised hypoactive sexual desire disorder that causes distress and is not explained by another listed cause.

The December 2025 US Addyi label covers eligible women younger than 65, including certain postmenopausal patients. Vyleesi remains indicated for eligible premenopausal women. Neither is simply hormone replacement or a general sexual-performance enhancer. Local authorisation and the current label must be checked.

Addyi has important alcohol-timing, interaction, low-blood-pressure and fainting precautions, and is contraindicated with liver impairment and certain interacting medicines. Vyleesi can raise blood pressure and is contraindicated with uncontrolled hypertension or known cardiovascular disease. A qualified prescriber should assess the diagnosis, risks and expected benefit.

Slowing unwanted facial hair

Eflornithine cream is a prescription option for slowing unwanted facial-hair growth where it is available. It does not remove hair that is already present, and its effect takes time. People may still use an appropriate hair-removal method while treating the rate of new growth.

Depilatory creams, laser treatment and electrolysis address hair in different ways. Consider skin sensitivity, hair and skin colour, treatment expertise, expense and whether maintenance is likely. Sudden or rapidly increasing hair growth, especially with other androgen-related changes, deserves medical assessment rather than cosmetic treatment alone.

Natural and bioidentical do not mean risk-free

A plant-derived supplement, a compounded hormone mixture and a regulated bioidentical prescription are not the same thing. Bioidentical refers to chemical similarity to hormones made in the body; it does not prove that a product is safer or more effective. Some regulated prescription hormones are bioidentical.

ACOG recommends approved menopausal hormone therapies over routine use of compounded bioidentical products when suitable approved options exist. Supplements marketed for hormone balance may have uncertain ingredients, interactions or limited evidence. Bring the actual label to a pharmacist or clinician instead of treating the word natural as a safety guarantee.

Movement and food can support health without curing every cause

Yoga can support flexibility, strength, relaxation and wellbeing. Other enjoyable movement and an adequate, varied diet can also support overall health. These practices do not replace levothyroxine for an underactive thyroid or prove that a hormone disorder has resolved.

For some people, a supported change in weight can improve particular metabolic or reproductive outcomes. A fixed ten-percent weight-loss target is not a universal requirement, and useful lifestyle benefits can occur without weight loss. Men with erectile difficulties also need an appropriate assessment rather than being told weight alone explains the problem. Care should fit nutrition, disability, resources, preferences and any eating-disorder history.

Practical comfort measures for dryness and hot flushes

For vaginal discomfort, choose a lubricant or moisturiser intended for that use and stop a product that irritates. A source’s blanket rule to avoid every product containing glycerin or parabens does not establish that all such products are unsafe. Oil-based products can damage latex barriers; check compatibility and the instructions.

Some people notice that heat, spicy food or hot drinks trigger flushing. Adjusting an individual trigger, choosing comfortable layers and keeping the sleeping area comfortable may help. These measures are optional supports, not proof that you caused symptoms through food choices. Persistent pain, unusual discharge or bleeding needs assessment.

Why acne can change with hormones

Androgen effects on oil-producing glands contribute to acne, especially around puberty. Adult acne can also fluctuate around the menstrual cycle, although not everyone has a predictable pre-period pattern. Acne may affect the face, chest, upper back and shoulders and can coexist with otherwise normal hormone levels.

Treatment depends on lesion type, severity, scarring risk and pregnancy plans. Acne with markedly irregular periods or new excess hair may prompt investigation, while ordinary acne alone does not establish an endocrine disease. Avoid assuming that every flare can be fixed with contraception, an anti-androgen or a supplement.

Weight change needs context

Hormonal conditions can influence weight, but the direction, size and mechanism vary. Excess cortisol in Cushing syndrome can affect appetite and fat distribution. An underactive thyroid can contribute to weight gain. Menopause and ageing may coincide with changes in body composition, activity and energy needs.

These examples do not mean that an unexplained change in weight proves one of those diagnoses. Treatment of an identified condition may help, but it does not guarantee a particular weight change or make nutrition, sleep and other medical factors irrelevant. Rapid change, swelling or additional concerning symptoms should be assessed.

Normal pregnancy changes and endocrine disease are different

Pregnancy involves substantial normal hormonal changes. Calling all of them an imbalance can make an expected transition sound like an illness. At the same time, a pre-existing thyroid disorder, diabetes or another endocrine condition may need closer monitoring and a modified treatment plan.

Untreated or inadequately treated hypothyroidism can affect pregnancy and fetal development, including brain development. This is a reason for appropriate treatment and follow-up, not a prediction that every baby will have a birth defect. Discuss medicines before conception when possible and contact the maternity and treating teams early after a positive test.

PCOS or PMOS does not rule out pregnancy

Irregular or absent ovulation can make conception harder in this syndrome, but many people conceive with or without treatment. Fertility assessment considers ovulation alongside factors such as sperm and tubal function. Support with metabolic health may help, but delaying all fertility care until a prescribed weight target is reached is not an automatic rule.

The international guideline recommends letrozole first for suitable anovulatory infertility without other infertility factors. Its licensing varies. Selected second-line options include gonadotrophins or laparoscopic ovarian surgery in appropriate circumstances; surgery is not a routine step after failed IVF. IVF may follow unsuccessful earlier treatment or be indicated for another fertility reason. Decisions and monitoring belong with a fertility team.

Plan pregnancy monitoring around the actual risks

PCOS or PMOS is associated with increased risks including miscarriage, gestational diabetes, hypertensive disorders, preterm birth and some fetal-growth concerns. This does not mean complications are inevitable. Tell the maternity team about the diagnosis so preconception assessment and pregnancy monitoring can be tailored.

The international guideline does not regard the syndrome itself as increasing large-for-gestational-age birth or macrosomia risk. That corrects a common overgeneralisation; diabetes and other individual circumstances still matter. Caesarean birth or neonatal care may be needed for specific complications, but the diagnosis alone does not determine the birth plan.

Hair loss can involve hormones and genetics together

Hereditary pattern hair loss is not completely separate from hormones. Androgenetic alopecia involves genetic susceptibility and androgen-related biology, particularly in male-pattern hair loss; mechanisms in women are more complex. A family history does not exclude a hormone-related contribution.

Thyroid disease and changes around pregnancy, the postpartum period or menopause can also be relevant to shedding or thinning. Scalp disease, nutritional problems and other illnesses are additional possibilities. The pattern, timing and scalp examination help distinguish them. New patchy loss, scalp inflammation or persistent shedding deserves a proper diagnosis before buying a hormone treatment.

Complications depend on the diagnosed condition

Endocrine disorders are not one disease with one inevitable complication list. Type 1 and type 2 diabetes involve different mechanisms; diabetes insipidus concerns water balance and is distinct from blood-glucose diabetes. High blood pressure, abnormal cholesterol, cardiovascular or kidney disease and sleep apnoea may coexist with particular conditions, but are not outcomes everyone with a hormone symptom should expect.

Some disorders can affect bone strength, muscle, fertility, sexual function or thyroid size, including a goitre. Long gaps between periods from persistent anovulation may require endometrial protection. Breast and endometrial cancer risks have specific mechanisms and risk factors; it is misleading to claim that a vague imbalance generally causes both.

Depression, anxiety, poor sleep and urinary symptoms also have many possible contributors. They deserve care in their own right and should not be dismissed while waiting for a hormone test. Identifying the actual diagnosis makes monitoring and prevention more useful than reading a long list of possible diseases.

Prepare for a useful consultation and follow-up

Record the symptoms that bother you, when they started, cycle or pregnancy changes, current medicines and supplements, and any relevant family history. Bring previous results rather than repeatedly ordering broad panels without context. Primary care can begin many assessments and arrange endocrinology, gynaecology, dermatology or fertility input when appropriate.

Agree on what treatment is intended to improve, how benefit will be measured and when to review it. Seek prompt help for a rapidly worsening problem; emergency symptoms such as collapse, chest pain or severe confusion should not wait for a hormone appointment. Do not stop an essential medicine or start a prescription hormone based only on a general article.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Match treatment to a diagnosed condition and a defined goal. Symptoms and one test result rarely establish the full explanation.

Current prescribing information and professional guidance differ from several generalisations in older hormone-balance articles. Product approval, fertility pathways and monitoring must be localised.

How BeMama can help

Bring your symptoms, medicines and priorities to the appointment, and ask what each proposed treatment is meant to change.

When to seek help

Clinical review remains required. Pregnancy plans, medical history and interactions can substantially change whether a treatment is appropriate.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Different hormone-related conditions need different assessments and treatments.
  • Local vaginal treatment, systemic menopausal therapy and contraception are not interchangeable.
  • Natural or bioidentical labels do not establish safety.
  • Fertility care and pregnancy monitoring should follow the actual diagnosis and individual risks.

Frequently asked questions

Is there one medicine that balances all hormones?

No. Treatment depends on the diagnosis and the outcome you want to improve. Replacement hormones, contraception, metabolic treatment and symptom relief have different purposes.

Is vaginal oestrogen the same as full-body hormone therapy?

No. Low-dose vaginal treatment primarily addresses local symptoms and has less systemic absorption. It generally does not treat hot flushes. Individual prescribing precautions still matter.

Can testosterone help anyone who feels tired?

No. Appropriate treatment requires symptoms, consistently low levels confirmed with suitable testing and investigation of the cause. It can suppress sperm production and needs monitoring.

Does metformin treat every PCOS symptom?

No. It has a particular metabolic role and selected reproductive uses. Other treatments may be more appropriate for acne, excess hair or ovulation, depending on the situation.

Are Addyi and Vyleesi only for premenopausal women?

Their US labels now differ. The December 2025 Addyi label includes eligible women under 65, including certain postmenopausal patients. Vyleesi remains for eligible premenopausal women. Neither is suitable for every cause of low desire.

Will eflornithine remove facial hair immediately?

No. It slows new facial-hair growth rather than removing existing hair, and its effect takes time. Discuss other suitable hair-removal methods and any need to investigate the cause.

Are compounded bioidentical hormones safer because they are natural?

That has not been established. Some approved medicines are bioidentical, but that is different from a compounded mixture or a plant supplement. Product quality, evidence and personal risks matter.

Must ovarian surgery come after failed IVF?

No. In selected anovulatory PCOS or PMOS infertility, laparoscopic ovarian surgery can be a second-line option. IVF may follow earlier treatment failure or be indicated for another reason. A specialist should individualise the sequence.

Does PCOS always mean a large baby or a caesarean?

No. The guideline does not attribute increased macrosomia risk to the syndrome itself, and the diagnosis does not predetermine the birth method. Other risks and individual conditions guide monitoring and care.

Should I stop thyroid medicine when I become pregnant?

No. Contact your treating team promptly for monitoring and dose advice. Appropriate thyroid treatment is important during pregnancy; do not stop or change it without clinical guidance.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
